translations.text: Account of the triumphs [?] of Mar Qardagh, the victorious [?] martyr.
My beloved, the accounts of the martyrs and saints of our Lord Jesus Christ are a benefit to the holy Church.
They are spiritual nourishment for the holy congregations of the cross.
They are an adornment to the lofty beauty of Christianity, sprinkled with the blood of the Son of God.
They are heavenly riches for all the generations who enter the holy Church through the spiritual birth of baptism.
They are a polished mirror in which discerning people see the inexpressible beauty of Christ.
They are treasures of righteousness for the children of the Church, who are called to the heavenly kingdom.
And the fire of Christ’s love blazes in the souls of believers.
Whoever eagerly desires to read them and continually reflect on them
is a beloved child of the saints, in whom their beauty in God finds expression.
(1) Relying on divine power, the sinful servant begins to write the account [?] of Mar Qardagh, whose name is sweet.
He was from the land of Assyria and of the lineage of Nimrod. Strengthen me with your power, Lord, so that through it I may reach completion.
Therefore, my beloved, I long to recount to you the wonderful triumphs and great contests of the athlete of righteousness,
the holy martyr Mar Qardagh, at whose great contests of martyrdom the angels were astonished and human beings marveled.
This holy Mar Qardagh came from a great family and from the royal line of the Assyrians.
His father descended from the renowned family of the house of Nimrod, and his mother from the renowned family of the house of Sennacherib.
He was born to pagan parents who had gone astray in the error of the religion of the Magi.
For his father was a man well known in the kingdom and renowned among the Magi. His name was Gushnawi.
The holy Mar Qardagh was handsome in appearance, large in stature, and physically strong.
He possessed a spirit skilled in warfare and clung vigorously to the error of paganism.
He was praised for his service throughout the whole region of the Persians. When he was about twenty-five years old,
word of his reputation and valor reached Shapur, king of the Persians, who sent for him to come to his court with great honor.
When the king gave the command and Qardagh entered his presence, he saw his handsome appearance and the strength
of his body and was greatly pleased with him. He ordered him to compete in the stadium before all the nobles of the kingdom
and to shoot an arrow at a small target fixed to the top of a tall pole.
They brought a bow and five arrows from the king’s armory. When he shot the five arrows at the target,
they all lodged in the same spot, and he was praised by the king and all his nobles.
The next day the king ordered him to come to the stadium and play ball with him and the rest of his nobles.
When this took place, the king and his nobles were greatly amazed at him.
On the third day the king went out hunting with a hundred nobles and three hundred horsemen.
He ordered him to ride with him on a horse from the king’s stables and to go before him at the head of the king’s armor-bearers.
As they were about to enter a forest, they saw ahead of them a doe running with her fawn.
Immediately the king shouted, saying, “Raise your bow with a strong hand, young Qardagh, and show your skill!”
He quickly took an arrow, set it on the bow, and drew it back forcefully. With a single arrow he brought down both the doe and her fawn.
Then the king shouted in a loud voice and said, “Long live Qardagh! Live and rejoice in your youth, and give us
joy through your victories!” As soon as the king returned from the hunt, he gave orders, and they gave him magnificent gifts.
He made him viceroy of Assyria and appointed him frontier governor from the River Turmara to the city of Nisibis.
He sent him off with great ceremony, also sending magnificent gifts and honors to his father through him.
When he reached the territories under his authority, the Christian people were greatly alarmed by him,
for they knew his boundless zeal for the error of the Magian religion.
Fervent prayer concerning him was offered before God throughout the whole church,
that he, the Almighty, would restrain his fury and not allow him to stir up persecution against the Christians.
For they were being severely persecuted during the reign of Shapur, who thirsted for the blood of the saints.
When he entered his home in Arbela, the city of the Assyrians, he held a great festival for the gods of the pagans.
He greatly honored the Magian religion and gave generous gifts to the fire temples.
After a few days he began building a fortress and a house on a hill called Malqi.
In two years he built and completed a strong fortress and a beautiful house.
Below the hill he built a fire temple at great expense and appointed Magi there to tend the fire. While he was building
that fortress, one night, as he was asleep,
he saw in his dream a young horseman, dressed and equipped in his armor, mounted on a horse and standing above him.
He prodded him in the side with the butt of his spear and said to him, “Qardagh!” He answered, “Here I am.”
He said to him, “Know for certain that before this fortress you are to die as a martyr for Christ.”
Qardagh said to him, “Who are you, to predict these things for me?” The blessed man said to him:
“I am Sergius, the servant of Christ. I am not telling your fortune, as you suppose;
rather, I have told you beforehand what is to come, just as Christ my Lord made it known to me.”
When Qardagh awoke from his sleep, he was greatly afraid, and he told his mother the dream in private.
His mother said to him, “Take heed, my son: do not mistreat the Christians.
For I am certain that they are people who worship the one true God, and their God has shown you this dream.”
But he paid no attention. Now there was a certain blessed man whose name was Abdisho.
He lived in a cave on a mountain in the region of Beth Bgash.
He was a man of great virtue, and in revelations
from God he found delight. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Get up, go down, and appear before Qardagh the marzban,
for through your hands I will win him into my household. For he must suffer greatly for my name.”
The blessed Abdisho got up and took his staff in his hand.
He carried the holy Gospel in a small bag and went down as he had been commanded.
One day, as Qardagh was going out to the stadium to play ball,
the holy Abdisho met him and crossed the road in front of him.
When he saw him cross in front of him, he became very angry and said to those accompanying him, “This man is a bad omen.”
He ordered two soldiers to strike the holy Mar Abdisho in the face.
After they had flogged him severely, he ordered that he be held in custody until he decided on a fitting punishment for him.
Qardagh himself returned home. After staying a little while, he got up and mounted again to go to the stadium.
But the holy Abdisho burned with zeal for God. He raised his hand, made the sign of the cross, and said:
“Lord God Almighty, show him your glory and reveal your power to him,
so that he may know that you are the true God, and there is no other besides you, just as you showed me in the revelation.”
When they reached the stadium and began to strike the ball while galloping on their horses, the ball stuck to the ground, and did not
They were able to move it from its place.
Immediately he ordered one of the workers to go down, take the ball in his hand, and throw it far away.
But when he picked it up from the ground and threw it forcefully, it fell in front of his feet.
All his workers did this, one after another, but accomplished nothing.
Then they were astonished and said, “That man who met us really is a sorcerer!
He has bound our ball with his sorcery and spoiled our enjoyment.”
But one of them replied, “While we were preparing to mount,
I saw that man raise his right hand and make the sign of the Christians’ cross.
His lips were moving as though he were whispering something.”
Then the governor turned back and entered his house, astonished and amazed at what had happened, as were all those with him.
As soon as he sat down, he gave an order, and they brought Saint Abdisho before him.
He questioned him angrily, saying, “Where are you from, man? And what is your occupation?” The blessed Abdisho answered him:
“As I have heard from my parents, they came from Haza, a village in the land of the Assyrians. And because they were Christians,
they were driven out by the misguided pagans and went to live in the village of Tamanon, in the land of the Carduchians.
But I have no fixed place or particular dwelling.
For I have heard concerning Christ my Lord, who came and redeemed us by his holy death, that he had nowhere to lay his head,
even though heaven and earth, and those above and those below, belong to him, and he holds, governs, and preserves them.
My occupation is to offer praise without ceasing and give thanks to God, our maker and provider,
who created us in his image and [?] in his likeness, and redeemed us through his Only Begotten, who clothed himself in our flesh,
and gave us knowledge and understanding, so that we would not regard created things as gods or offer worship—
which is owed to him alone—to created things that came into being and were fashioned by him, as you misguided pagans do.”
When Qardagh heard this, he became very angry and ordered them to strike the saint on the mouth.
While the blessed Abdisho was being severely beaten, his eyes were fixed on heaven.
He prayed silently to God to fulfill in deed what he had told him in a revelation.
Qardagh said to him angrily, “Why are you calling
Us, worshippers of created things, you foolish old man? But the blessed Abdisho remained silent and did not answer him a word.
Qardagh said to him: Will you not answer me? Do you not know that I have authority over your death and your life? But the blessed Abdisho said to him:
I suppose, my lord, that when someone is struck on the mouth, he is being taught this:
that he ought not to speak. That is why I did not give Your Excellency an answer.
But what you said—that you have authority over my death and my life—is not true. You have authority to kill the body,
but we, the servants of Christ and worshippers of the cross, do not consider this death, but true and immortal life.
But over my soul and my life in Christ you have no authority at all.
Our Lord encouraged us and commanded us in his [?], saying: Do not fear those who kill the body,
but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear me, for I can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.
But if you want me to speak with you, calm your anger, compose yourself, and listen to me kindly,
and order them not to strike me again. Then Qardagh swore to him, saying:
Say whatever you wish, and no one will strike you again. Then the holy Abdisho answered
and said to him: Do you agree that whatever is self-existent and was not made
is the true God? The governor said to him: Yes, I agree.
The blessed man said to him: And do you acknowledge that whatever was made and is not self-existent
is a created thing? The governor said to him: Yes, that is what I acknowledge.
The blessed man said to him again: And do you know that created things should not be worshipped, and that whoever worships created things
angers God their Creator? The governor said to him: Yes, my lord, you have spoken truly, and that is how it is.
But show me: who worships created things? The blessed man said to him:
You and all your pagan companions worship created things.
The governor said to him: If you show me that I worship created things and anger God,
I will gladly agree with you and follow your teaching, and I will consider it the greatest favor you could do me.
But if you do not show me, know and understand that you are truly insulting me.
The blessed man said to him: Do you not worship the sun, the moon, fire, water, air, and earth,
and call them gods and goddesses? Qardagh said to him: Yes, I worship them, because they are self-existent and were not made.
The blessed man said to him, “Where, then, did you discover that the heavenly lights are self-existent and not created?” Qardagh said to him:
“From their ceaseless courses, from the unchanging character of their nature, and from the fact
that they persist in the power of their nature and do not change like everything else, and that they are set high above.”
The blessed man said to him, “These things you have mentioned they received from their Creator when they were formed; they are no grounds for praising the heavenly lights themselves.
That they are not self-existent is evident from the fact that they are not even alive. But if you say that they are alive,
I will ask you a question; answer me: what sort of life do they possess—that of animals or that of rational beings? If they possess the life of animals,
why are they not nourished like animals? Or are they perhaps rational and discerning? And if you say that they are rational and discerning,
why do they not sometimes draw back their heat and rest from their course? For if the sun were rational,
it would put an end to the harshness of the cold in winter, and in summer it would not increase its heat.
In a place colder than another it would bring relief, and where it is hot it would draw back its rays.
It would grow tired and suffer in its ceaseless course. For everything that is alive and visible and moves by [?] also grows tired.
And everything that is not alive and does not grow tired is moved by something else.
A stone, an arrow, and a cart are moved by others and do not grow tired, because they are not alive. But a bird
and animals move on their own and grow tired, because they are alive.
If [?], then, the heavenly lights and the elements move on their own, they also grow tired and suffer, because they are visible.
But since they do not move on their own—as it is also evident that they are without sensation and without a soul—for this reason they do not grow tired.
They are moved by the [?] of others, like a stone, an arrow, and carts.
The former—that is, the heavenly lights and the elements—are moved by God; the latter—that is, a stone, an arrow, and the rest—are moved by us.”
The governor said to him, “And why, unlike these things on earth, do they possess ceaseless motion,
light, and power that is free from change, decay, and hindrance?” The blessed man said to him:
“Because they have the same rank as the principal organs in the body, such as the brain, the heart, and the liver.
For example, if someone removes a nail, a hair, or a tooth from the body, it is a partial loss.
But if someone removes the brain, the heart, or the liver, the loss of such organs destroys the whole life.
Likewise, if one of these things that are small parts of the world’s [?] constitution perishes,
such as animals and plants, it is a partial loss.
But if the Creator had allowed the heavenly lights to perish, it would have meant the destruction of the world
as a whole. For the heavenly lights support the whole body of creation: they are its chief organs, the eyes and brain of the world.
From them comes all the warmth in bodies and in plants,
as well as the ordering of the seasons and the counting of years, months, weeks, and days.
Yet they do not possess these things independently, as their own masters, but received them from the [?] and wisdom of their Creator, although they are neither alive nor capable of sensation.
And just as, if ten people are in one house and one of them suffers damage to his sight,
he alone suffers in darkness [?], while the others are free from pain,
if you extinguish the lamp inside the house or shut the door, the ordeal of the punishment reaches everyone in the house.
Such is the loss of these other things in comparison with the loss of the heavenly lights.
From this it has become clear that the heavenly lights are not self-existent but made, and that they are neither alive nor capable of sensation.
Whoever worships them angers God their Creator. The same is true of the elements:
I mean earth, water, fire, and air. They are made, and are neither alive nor capable of sensation.
How can they be called self-existent when they are dissolved and destroyed by one another? The victory of each one of them is the defeat of its fellow.
For earth is dissolved by water and is also swept away. And water is swallowed up by
earth and disappears; it is also dispersed by air. Fire is extinguished by water and perishes,
and air is confined in a waterskin and heated by the heavenly lights, while foulness and stagnation become mixed into it.
In short, each and every one of them is, in and of itself, destructive of everything, including its fellow.
They are dissolved and changed, and depend on one another.
Everything that is dependent has come into being, and everything that has not come into being is not dependent.
For just as what has not come into being needs nothing at all, so too everything that has come into being is dependent.
Experience itself testifies that the elements are dependent,
and that none of them can contribute to the common good without its fellow.
For earth needs water to produce growth, and water needs air to lift it up and sprinkle it down.
Fire, in turn, cannot display its activity without wood, which grows through earth, water, and air.
Thus it has become clear that they are dependent. And if they depend on one another, they too have come into being.
For the self-existent one depends neither on himself nor on others.
And is not the self-existent one living and also rational? For the elements are neither living nor rational. For everything that is alive
and visible moves by itself and has sensation.
For the elements are not only without reason; they are also without life or sensation.
For plants, like animals, have life: plants grow and sprout,
while animals have movement and the ability to change location, together with sensory perception.
But the elements have none of these things; rather, they are motionless like stones.
Anyone who worships these things and considers them self-existent angers God, their Creator.
So I rightly called you worshipers of created things and people far from God.
When the marzban heard these things, he became very angry, because his error would not allow him to be persuaded by the blessed man's words.
He ordered that Saint Abdisho be bound with heavy chains and imprisoned in a dark room.
A little bread was to be given to him each evening, but they were to give him no water.
The saint was bound and imprisoned, rejoicing and singing psalms, saying, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid.
What can a human being do to me?” The next day, the marzban went out to pursue game and hunt.
He drew his bow to shoot an arrow, but it fell before his feet. The same thing also happened to the soldiers with him.
Although they tried many times, the air would not carry the arrows that they
were shooting. When this happened to them, they were greatly afraid.
The marzban spoke and said to those with him, “I think that old man whom we have imprisoned is a man of God.
Through his prayers this wonder has happened, and our weapons have been restrained because we embittered him.”
He immediately turned back and entered his house in great distress. He spent the night without eating [?] or drinking.
He had resolved in his mind to release the blessed Abdisho in the morning.
At midnight, a great and glorious light filled the room where the blessed Abdisho was imprisoned.
A great company of spiritual beings appeared beside him, singing psalms in a loud voice and saying:
“The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them and delivered them.
The Lord is near to those who call on him in truth. He fulfills the desire of those who fear him; he hears their plea and saves them.”
The blessed Abdisho himself was also singing joyfully with them.
And great fear fell upon all those who were nearby, around the house where the blessed man was imprisoned.
Immediately all the doors opened, and the angel of the Lord approached the blessed man's chains.
The chains fell from his hands and feet, and the angel took him by the hand, led him away, and brought him out of the prison.
When he had brought him outside, he let go of his hand and said to him, “Come
after me.” He went ahead of him in splendid clothes until he brought him into his cave. Then he left him and departed.
When morning came, the governor ordered them to unbind the holy man and bring him before him.
When those who had been sent opened the doors and went in, they found only the chains lying there.
And the fragrance of fine spices filled the whole house.
When they searched for the blessed man and did not find him, they were astonished and became very afraid.
They hurriedly ran and informed the governor, saying, “My lord, we went as you commanded,
and found the doors shut. We opened them and went in, and found these chains lying there,
and the house was full of the fragrance of perfumes, but we did not find the man.”
When the governor heard these things, he fell into great fear and distress.
He struck his face and wept bitterly, saying, “Woe to me! Woe to me!
Woe to me, for I have tormented the man of God! Truly, the God of the Christians is great!
He is the true God who made heaven and earth and everything in them, and there is no other god besides him!”
Immediately he got up, entered the bedroom, and scratched the sign of the cross on the eastern wall.
He fell face down on the ground and prayed before it, saying, “Christ, God
of the Christians, answer me and seek me out, and do not reject me. Make me worthy to be counted among your worshipers and to be marked with the holy seal.
I have believed and confessed, and I confess that you are the true God, just as your Christian worshipers confess and teach.
If, then, the one who appeared to me in human form was a human being,
and spoke with me in your name, and I offended him in my ignorance, make me worthy, my Lord, to see him again,
and to ask him for forgiveness of my offenses, and through his hands to be brought to know you and to belong to your household.
And if the one who appeared to me in human form was one of your holy angels,
Let him appear to me again and teach me what I ought to do.
As soon as he finished his prayer and marked himself with the sign of the cross, a pleasant, gentle voice was heard saying to him:
“For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks the door will be opened.”
When he heard that voice, he was comforted and rejoiced greatly. His soul was glad, and he praised God.
He went out and sat on his couch, ate some food, and regained his strength.
Now the Magian priest who used to perform the Magian rites for him whenever he ate, together with his wife and all the members of his household,
were amazed and astonished at him because he ate bread without having the Magian rites performed for him.
But no one dared question him, for he was very stern and harsh toward the members of his household.
After three days, Saint Mar Abdisho appeared to him in a vision at night, joyful and cheerful, and said to him:
“My son Qardagh, if you want to see me, come to such-and-such a cave, and you will find me there.”
When he awoke from his sleep, he rejoiced greatly, and his soul was glad.
In the morning he rose joyfully, changed his clothes, and disguised himself.
He took with him two faithful servants whom he trusted to keep his secrets,
who had also been deemed worthy, along with him, of the gift of baptism.
He mounted and rode joyfully toward the region of Beth Bgash, to the mountain where Saint Abdisho lived,
where he had arranged to meet him in the vision. When he had gone about five miles from his fortress,
Satan met him in the form of an old man, angry and gloomy, holding his beard between his teeth, and said to him:
“Where are you going, you liar, you wicked man? Why have you betrayed me and abandoned me and gone after that accursed white-haired man, the disciple of Jesus,
whom our companions the Jews crucified in Jerusalem, and who died? I have sworn, and I am not lying, that I will stir up against you the king
and all the nobles of Persia, and I will shed your blood like that of robbers and evildoers.”
When one of his servants heard this, he said to his master, “Shall I draw my sword and cut off the head of this old dog,
who has dared to insult our master?” Then his master said to him, “Leave him alone, for he will not fall before a sword.
Our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom I have believed, will destroy him with the breath of his mouth and bring him to nothing by the revelation of his coming.
For this is what I have heard Christians say about him.”
For Saint Mar Qardagh had understood that it was Satan who had appeared to him in human form.
Immediately he spat at him and said to him, “May Christ my Lord rebuke you, he who in his grace rescued me from the darkness of error,
and called me and brought me near to the great light of knowing him.” And he marked himself with the sign of the cross.
When Satan heard the name of Christ, he immediately changed his form and became like a black snake, and fled into a crack in the rock.
But the blessed Qardagh continued on his way, rejoicing and praising God.
While he was at a lodging place along the way, Saint Sergius the martyr appeared to him in a dream and said to him, “My brother Qardagh,
you have begun well. Fight bravely, so that you may be
my brother forever. See, I am with you to help you until you reach fulfillment and receive the crown of martyrdom.”
The next day, toward evening, as he began to approach the mountain where Saint Abdisho lived,
an angel of the Lord appeared to Saint Abdisho and said to him, “Get up and go out to meet Qardagh the marzban,
and welcome him joyfully, for I have chosen him, says the Lord, and he is mine, and he is destined to suffer much for my sake.”
Saint Abdisho rose joyfully, holding his staff in his hand and the holy book of the Gospel on his left arm.
As he walked, he sang a psalm, saying, “He who carries seed goes on his way weeping.
He who carries a sheaf will surely come with joy.” When he saw the blessed Qardagh from a distance,
he spoke to him cheerfully, saying, “Your bonds are very weak, my lord marzban.
To us, who are bound by the Holy Spirit and journey toward heaven, they count for nothing.
But this is how the great men and rulers of the world welcome strangers who come to them!”
The blessed Qardagh answered him with great joy, saying, “Although we bound you while we were in error,
you nevertheless freed us from the fetters of paganism and were patient with us,
so that we might come and ask your forgiveness. And you, like a merciful father, will ask our Lord to pardon the sins we have committed against him.”
Immediately he dismounted from his horse and fell at Saint Abdisho’s feet, weeping and saying, “Forgive me, my lord, servant of God.
And plead with Christ my Lord to make me worthy to be perfected in his love.” The blessed man took him by the hand and said to him, “Get up.”
He rose, and Abdisho kissed him and said to him, “Welcome, my son, whom I fathered in my bonds. Our Lord Jesus Christ is waiting for you,
and his holy angels rejoice over you.” Then the young men led the mount to a monastery,
which stood at the foot of the mountain, having been instructed not to say who owned the mount.
The two of them went up to the cave where Saint Abdisho lived.
When the time came, the blessed Abdisho stood up to chant the evening service.
The blessed Qardagh stood beside him with reverence and great joy.
Suddenly a band of vicious demons appeared on the cliff above them,
dancing, clapping their hands, laughing, and saying, “Oh, how fine it is for the viceroy and frontier governor,
having left his house, his honor, his authority, and his high position, to spend the night hungry among the cliffs with misguided people
who live in caves!” But the blessed Abdisho did not stop his service.
Instead, he signaled to Saint Mar Qardagh to give them a fitting answer.
The blessed man answered them, “You are always liars and fathers of falsehood.
But in this you have spoken the truth: it is indeed good for the viceroy and frontier governor
to delight in spiritual nourishment full of true life, together with holy people
who have overcome your cunning schemes through their words. They have abandoned the earth and are hastening toward heaven.
But when, in accordance with your unclean will, I delighted in richly prepared tables and clarified wines,
I was deprived of the pure table of life in Christ and was far from God.
I had become a companion of you dark and rebellious beings, who are kept for that torment which never ends.
But today, since Christ my Lord has made me worthy of the light of knowing him, I delight in the spiritual table of his holy teaching.
But you unclean beings, go into the outer darkness!” Immediately they departed, howling and shouting and shaking the mountain.
When the blessed men had finished their service and sat down, Saint Abdisho said to the blessed Qardagh, “Look, my son, we have
a few soaked chickpeas here and a little vinegar in a gourd. Let us eat, my son, and drink water.”
Qardagh answered him, “Whatever you wish, our father, I will gladly do.”
When they had prayed and begun to eat, an angel of the Lord appeared to them and said, “Peace be with you.”
As he spoke, he stretched out his hand, holding a loaf of fine bread.
He said to the blessed Qardagh, “When we came to you, you bound us in irons and gave us bread without water, barely enough to keep us alive.
But today, now that you have come to us, we have lodged you among high and beautiful mountains.
And look, we have brought you fine bread, and here is cold water flowing on the mountaintop.
But welcome in peace, for angels and human beings rejoice greatly at your coming to us.”
He placed the bread on the table and departed. The blessed men immediately stood up.
Both of them knelt for about three hours, praying, rejoicing, and praising God.
When they had finished their prayer, they ate what had been sent to them from heaven.
All night they devoted themselves to the service of God. Now there was an old man, advanced in years, whose name was
Beri. He lived in a cave about nine miles away from the cave of the blessed Abdisho.
He was a great and godly man, and he had lived on that mountain for sixty-eight years.
The Lord said to him in a vision, “Get up and go to Abdisho’s cave, and see Qardagh the marzban there.
Encourage him by your presence, and strengthen him with your words.”
The old man got up with great joy, and at daybreak he reached Abdisho’s cave.
When Abdisho saw him, he was astonished, for the old man had not left his cave for sixty-eight years.
The old man spoke to Abdisho and said, “Look, you have an important guest!
And why did you invite us to enjoy his company?” Abdisho said to him, “Forgive me, father.
I thought I should not trouble you in your old age—something that could not have happened anyway.”
The old man said to him, “Although you did not invite me, the Lord sent me.”
They prayed and greeted one another. The old man embraced Qardagh, kissed him, and said:
“Welcome, Esau, man of the open country, who has been transformed and become blameless Jacob, dwelling in the tent of the righteous!”
He sat down and spoke with him about the word of God until the ninth hour. Then he blessed him, kissed him, and got up and returned to his cave.
During the five days that the blessed Qardagh stayed with the holy Abdisho,
he earnestly begged him, night and day, to make him worthy of the seal of baptism.
On the night before the sixth day dawned, Saint Sergius the martyr appeared to Abdisho in a dream and said to him:
“Why are you delaying opening the door of martyrdom for my brother Qardagh?” When Abdisho awoke from his sleep,
he was greatly afraid. He called the blessed Qardagh and said to him, “Get up, my son.
Let us go down to the monastery where the young men are, and carry out what I was commanded to do tonight.”
As they were coming down from the mountain, the blessed Abdisho told Qardagh about the vision he had seen during the night.
When they reached the monastery, the brothers gathered and prepared for baptism.
With joy and gladness, he and his two young servants received the seal of Christ and shared in the holy mysteries.
After receiving the seal of baptism, he stayed with Saint Abdisho for seven days.
Then he set out and returned home, rejoicing in faith in Christ.
While he was at a lodging place along the road, Satan appeared to him in the form of a Magian,
with his clothes torn, wailing and weeping and saying, “Why, my son Qardagh, have you abandoned me and joined my enemies?” But the blessed man
said to him boldly, “I trust in the power of Christ my Lord
that I will rescue many from your destructive jaws and bring them to the house of worship of Christ my Lord.”
Satan answered him, “You have wretched men who live in caves,
but I have the kings and nobles of all Persia.
Now that you have betrayed me, I will go and inform the kings and rulers, and I will make you die a bitter death.”
But the blessed Qardagh marked himself with the sign of the cross and said to him:
“May Christ my Lord rebuke you! For love of him I am ready to suffer and die gladly.”
Immediately Satan changed his appearance and became like an old Ethiopian, with his hands on his head, wailing, weeping, and fleeing.
When the blessed man arrived home, he sent for a certain brother, a monk worthy of a good remembrance, whose name was Isaac.
Isaac taught him the psalms of the blessed David and read to him from the book of the holy Gospel.
From that time onward, the blessed man kept his mouth from eating meat.
From evening to evening he sustained himself on a fixed portion, seasoned with the flavors of rich foods.
He opened his treasuries and distributed large gifts and abundant alms to churches, convents, and holy monasteries,
and to the poor, the needy, orphans, and widows. And crowds
of sick people constantly gathered before him and at his gate. But his wife, his parents, and everyone in his household
were deeply distressed when they saw all the generosity he was showing.
The blessed man called them and said to them, “Why are you downcast, you foolish people,
over earthly possessions that are being stored up in heaven? Listen, if you are willing,
to the life-giving gospel of our Savior, which proclaims: ‘Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth,
where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.’
And where your treasure is, there your heart will also be.
So if you love me and belong to me, you too will be where I am.
And if you are not with me, then you are against me.
And do not grieve over my possessions, because I am giving them to Christ my Lord, who is the true king.
He became peaceful, and the holy man was gentle and kind toward the members of his household and toward everyone.
He gave up the battles and fighting in which he used to engage.
He stopped hunting, fishing, taking part in games in the stadium, and other such activities.
He devoted himself to fasting, worship, and reading the Scriptures.
He was also diligent in hearing legal cases and freeing the oppressed from
their oppressors, and rescuing those who were wronged from those who wronged them, throughout all the territories under his authority.
His father and mother lived in a district called Bar-Hewton,
because they had extensive possessions and estates there, and a renowned fire temple that they had built.
They lived in it. A little later, the blessed Qardagh himself made it into a large monastery,
which exists to this day and is called by his name. But when his parents heard that he had become a Christian
and was now dividing up his possessions and distributing his wealth to churches, monasteries, and the poor, they were deeply distressed.
His father said to the blessed man's mother, “A great calamity has befallen us, and we have become a curse among our peers.
While we thought we had a good heir, we had fathered and raised the destroyer of our household.”
But his mother said to her husband, “It seems to me that we should not hinder him. Instead, leave him to his own wishes,
and let him do whatever he wants. We have already grown old, and we must die.
The estates and possessions are his, and he has authority over what is his. Perhaps what he is doing is good? And if
we struggle to stop it, perhaps we are sinning.” But her husband rebuked her and said to her, “Be quiet, foolish woman!
I think you too are a Nazarene. Perhaps you are the one who has driven your son out of his mind.”
His father immediately wrote to him as follows: “Even though you have hated yourself and treated our lives [?] with contempt,
and have become a Nazarene, dishonored our family, and made us a disgrace among our peers,
nevertheless, you have no authority to distribute the possessions and estates of the fire temple to the Nazarenes.”
When the blessed man received his father's letter and read it, he laughed heartily and said, “Our old man is very foolish and is rushing toward hell.”
He wrote him this reply: “Old man, you worship fire, and in fire you will be tormented.
But I will give my possessions to Christ, because I will enjoy happiness with him. In him I place my hope, and on [?] I rely.
As for the fire temples in which you take pride, I will readily turn them into temples of Christ,
and I will set up splendid altars in them. I have no share or inheritance with you,
because Christ has called me, brought me near to himself, and made me a son of his hidden Father.”
But the wife of Saint Qardagh could not bear seeing the possessions scattered and gifts distributed.
She decided to write and inform her father, whose rank and office were Shahrkhwast Shapur Nekorgan.
After she had written a letter and was ready to send it the next morning,
that very night a handsome young man appeared to her in a dream,
dressed in white and seated on a golden throne at the gate of the blessed man's fortress.
He held a pen of fire and was writing letters on a broad white sheet of parchment and sealing them with his signet ring.
He sent them to heaven by the hands of beautiful young men dressed in white clothes, who flew on wings of fire.
When she saw that awesome vision and the young men going up to heaven and coming down to carry letters,
she approached him and asked, “Who are you, my lord? What is your work? And why are you sitting here
without the marzban being aware of you? And what are you writing?” He answered her,
“I am the commander of the armies of the Lord God, who made heaven and earth.
The great King of the ages sent me to record the gifts and alms given by
your husband and to send an account of them to heaven. As for your saying, ‘The marzban is not aware of you,’ you are certainly speaking falsely.
The marzban knows me and is aware that I am here. But you do not know me, because your heart is set on earthly things.”
When she woke from her sleep, she was filled with great fear.
Trembling, she ran to the blessed Qardagh and told him what she had seen.
She also showed him the letter she had written that evening to send to her father.
He said to her, “The vision you saw is indeed great, awesome, and true, but your own heart is hardened.
Our Lord said in his Gospel, ‘I have come to set a man against his father,’
and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's enemies will be the members of his own household.
And all this will go so far that even between a man and his wife, who are one flesh, there will be a rift and division.
This is what he said elsewhere: on that day when he is revealed in glory and brings about the resurrection,
and raises up the righteous and torments the wicked, two will be in one bed:
one will be taken to heaven, to the kingdom and to delight, and one will be left on earth, in Gehenna and torment.
But I trust in Christ my Lord that I too will go to him lightly laden, following my possessions.” And from that day on, no longer
did his wife dare to say anything to him, nor did she again show a gloomy face because of the blessed man's distribution of his possessions.
And when two years and three months had passed,
while Qardagh was conducting himself in all the good ways befitting true Christians,
the various peoples in the south and west heard about the change in the blessed man's way of life.
They learned that he had withdrawn from warfare, ceased fighting, and come to love a quiet life, and they made preparations,
all of them together—the Romans, the Arabs, and the other peoples around them.
They gathered like the sand on the seashore and set out to invade the territories under the blessed man's rule.
But a few days earlier he had gone up to the mountain to his teacher, Mar Abdisho.
After he had stayed with him for a month, while the two of them were making the previously mentioned visit to the holy elder Beri the ascetic,
the Romans and Arabs formed large raiding forces, took captives, and devastated all the territories under the blessed man's rule,
from the river Tormara as far as Nisibis, the city on the frontier. They also took captive his father and mother,
his wife, his brother and sister, and all the members of his household. There escaped,
however, from among his soldiers, two hundred and thirty-five mounted men.
They hurried to the mountain and searched for the blessed man.
They went and found him in the cave of Beri the ascetic with his teacher Abdisho and a large gathering of priests who had assembled to honor him.
When the blessed Qardagh saw them, he immediately spoke first and said to them, “You look to me like men who have escaped from a raiding force.”
One of them, a man brutish in his behavior and wicked in his paganism, answered him:
“When governors and frontier commanders live in the caves of thieves and deceivers, it was only fitting that this should happen to us.”
As he spoke these words, the angel of the Lord struck him, and he fell where he stood and died.
When his companions saw what had happened, they were very afraid.
They all believed in our Lord Jesus Christ and received the seal of holy baptism that very day.
Then blessed Qardagh said to the blessed saints Beri and Abdisho, “My fathers and masters,
pray for me, that I may go and, through the power of Christ our Lord and through your prayers, bring back the great company of captives from the plunderers.”
They marked him with the sign of the cross, kissed him, and sent him away in peace.
When he reached his fortress at Melqi and saw the ruins lying there, and his house plundered with no one left in it, he was deeply distressed.
He immediately sent swift messengers after them and wrote to them as follows:
“You thought that I, Qardagh, had cast off my former strength and prowess in battle,
and for this reason you dared to enter and devastate the territories under my authority.
But know this: I have certainly not cast it off; rather, I have put on strength that cannot be overcome.
Send me back all the people you have taken captive. Keep the possessions for yourselves and go in peace.
Do not stir up war with me; this is in your own interest.”
When they received and read the letters, they wrote back to him with insults, abuse, and mocking words.
He wrote to them again as follows: “But since I have put on Christ, the peace of the world,
I do not wish to clothe myself willingly in the fury of battle.
Instead, send me my father, my mother, my wife, my brother, my sister, and all the members of my household,
along with all the captives you carried off from the territories under my authority.
Keep the possessions for yourselves, turn aside, and leave me alone. Do not make me pursue you.” But when they heard
these things, feeling confident because they had already reached the territories under their own authority, they cut off his brother’s head and sent it to him.
When the blessed man saw his brother’s severed head, he was tormented with grief and burned with anger.
He immediately gave the command, and the horn sounded. He entered the church of God with two hundred and thirty-four soldiers and seven of his servants.
He stretched out his hands and prayed, saying, “Plead my cause, Lord, and fight against those who fight against me.
Take up weapons and a shield, and rise to help me. Draw the sword and make it flash against my pursuers.
Say to my soul, ‘I am your savior.’” When he had finished his prayer,
he took blessed dust from before the sanctuary and scattered it over his armor, his horse, and his soldiers.
And he hung around his neck a golden cross in which the holy wood of our Savior’s cross was set.
He raised his hands, directed his holy gaze toward heaven, and made a vow to the Lord, saying:
“Lord God, mighty one, warrior of the ages, if you will be with me on this journey that I am undertaking,
and by your power and help I overtake my enemies and defeat them,
and recover from them the captives they have taken, and return safely from the battle
that lies before me, I will uproot the fire temples and build shrines to the martyrs.
I will demolish the fire altars and establish holy altars in their places.
And the boys, the sons of the Magi, who have been set apart by their fathers as servants of Satan,
I will give as servants to Christ, and I will make them members of the covenant.
And the treasures and revenues that my ancestors set aside and gave to the fire temples, I will distribute to churches and monasteries.”
When he had finished the words of his vow and the declarations of his pledge, suddenly a voice was heard from the Lord’s sanctuary, saying:
“Take courage! Take courage! Be strong and steadfast, and do not be afraid, my servant Qardagh.
For I am with you, and I will deliver your enemies into your hands.” When that voice was heard,
he and his soldiers immediately fell facedown before the ark of the Lord for about two hours.
Then they rose joyfully and praised God. The holy man gave the order, the horn sounded three times, and they mounted.
Then one of his armor-bearers said, “But look, my lord, we do not know which road we should take to pursue our enemies.”
But the blessed man laughed cheerfully and said to him, “The one who let us hear the voice of victory will himself show us the right road to travel,
so that we may pursue and overtake our enemies.” When they had traveled about two miles, there were scraps from his wife’s silk garments lying on the road.
For she had acted with great wisdom: throughout the territory through which the captors traveled, at intervals of one parasang
or two parasangs, she would secretly steal an opportunity, unseen by the captors, tear scraps from the silk of her clothing,
and throw them onto the road, so that they would serve as signs and markers for her husband as he traveled in pursuit of them.
For she trusted in her husband’s readiness, determination, and compassion,
believing that he would not neglect to pursue the captors. When the blessed man saw this, he rejoiced greatly and praised God.
They followed those markers until they approached the territory of the Kurds.
He raised his eyes and saw great enemy armies encamped beside the River Khabur.
For they were encamped without fear, eating, drinking, singing, rejoicing, and delighting in the great number of captives and the vast plunder in their hands.
Then the blessed man dismounted from his horse, as did his soldiers, and they fell facedown on the ground. He prayed, saying:
“Heavenly King of kings, to whom belong the unchanging kingdom, power, authority, and might in heaven and on earth,
by whose power Joshua son of Nun destroyed great and mighty kings,
and by whose uplifted arm blessed David conquered the nations all around him, help us in our weakness,
so that your great name may be glorified through the victory of your worshipers forever and ever. Amen.” And all his soldiers answered with one voice, “Amen.”
The blessed man gave the order, and three horns sounded loud and terrifying blasts.
At that moment, his teacher, Saint Mar Abdisho, appeared to the blessed Qardagh,
holding the glorious sign of the cross in his hand, running before him, and saying to him, “Look, my son, here is the great sign of your victory!
Be strong and courageous, for the Lord has delivered your enemies into your hands.”
Suddenly the victorious man appeared before the enemies like terrifying lightning,
like the sun at its rising, and like a mighty warrior rejoicing to run his course.
Three times he shouted fiercely and said to them, “This is the day of repayment for your insolence, you unclean dogs!”
Immediately he blazed into battle. All the captives ran to meet the blessed man and took their place behind him.
The troops scattered before him, and he cut them down like ears of grain in a field.
Their corpses fell into the River Khabur like floating locusts, and a few of them escaped on foot to the mountain.
He struck them down and pursued them as far as the foot of the mountain on whose summit the ark of Noah’s household had rested [?].
The holy man returned with great victory and joy, singing and saying:
“Some rely on chariots and some on horses, but we will be strong in the name of the Lord our God.
They bowed down and fell, but we rose and stood ready, because the Lord our God saved us.”
He turned back and plundered the camps, brought away the spoils, and brought back all the captives.
When they came to Beth Bawta, he gave the order, and the horn sounded.
All his soldiers assembled, and he inspected them and found that they had all been kept safe and unharmed.
As soon as the blessed man reached his home, he gave orders, and the fire temples that had been built for his ancestors were torn down.
He made them holy sanctuaries for the Most High. He overturned the fire altars in which the fire had been kept burning by the misguided Magi.
And he [?] splendid altars for Christ. Everything he had vowed to the Lord he completed and fulfilled with
great joy. Now when the Magi in the territories under his authority saw all these things,
they wrote secretly and informed a certain Magus who was called Mobadan Mobad.
He immediately went in to King Shapur and said to him, “My lord the king, live forever!
That Qardagh who was so greatly honored by Your Majesty,
and whom you made viceroy of Assyria and frontier governor in the western region, has joined the religion of the Nazarenes.
He has demolished the fire temples and built churches and monasteries.
He flogs the Magi and makes them become Nazarenes. He has scorned the worship of the gods,
insulted the great teaching of the Magian religion, and regarded your kingdom as a widow without a husband.”
When the king heard this, he said to him angrily, “How have you heard these things, yet that whole great victory that Qardagh won—
how, with two hundred and thirty-four men, he destroyed thousands of Romans and tens of thousands of Arabs—
have you not heard of it?” When the Magus heard these words from the king, he trembled and became afraid. He remained silent and said nothing.
Distressed and dejected, he left the king’s presence and went and gathered all the nobles of the kingdom.
With his words he stirred them up to accuse the blessed Qardagh before the king together, as one assembly.
Then they all gathered and unanimously sent a message
to the king, saying, “Our lord the king, if it pleases your gracious will that paganism should be destroyed and abolished,
and that we should all become Nazarenes, give orders for your will to be made known to your servants, so that we may know what we ought to do.
But if this is not so, why have you disregarded the insolent Qardagh?
Look, he insults the gods, demolishes the fire temples, and builds houses of worship for the evil religion of the Nazarenes.”
When the king heard these things, he was deeply distressed, because he loved the blessed Qardagh with all his soul.
But because of the nobles’ wishes, he was compelled to summon the blessed Qardagh.
He immediately gave orders, and a letter was written to the holy Qardagh as follows:
“We have heard about the victory and heroic deeds you accomplished against the Romans, the Arabs, and the other peoples
who dared to invade our dominion, our good servant.
Therefore we have been pleased to enjoy the sight of you and to reward you with honor for your great victory.”
But when you see this royal letter of ours, come promptly to our court, and do not delay.
For the king was afraid to inform him openly about the matter, lest he rebel, cause an uprising, and shake the kingdom.
When the blessed man received the king’s letter and read it, he laughed softly and said to the man who had brought it, “What
the letter says is not what the king has in his heart. Yet he has spoken the truth:
I am to receive great honors and burning gifts from his hands, and I am ready to go with great joy.”
Immediately he entered the church, spread out the letter before the Lord, and prayed, saying, “Christ, Son of God,
who bought his church with his innocent blood, did away with sin, and made me, a sinner, worthy to belong to his household:
strengthen me in my weakness to stand firm in this great contest set before me.
Grant that I may emerge from it victorious and die for your name, with my mouth full of thanksgiving to you and praise of your holy name.”
He marked himself with the sign of the cross and set out, praising God.
When he arrived at the king’s court, the king secretly sent him a message, saying:
“Look, the Magi and all the nobles of the kingdom are threatening you and want to kill you,
because they have heard that you abandoned the religion of the Magi and the worship of the gods and became a Christian.
But when you come before me, do not say that you are a Christian,
so that your accusers may be put to shame, and we will bestow great honors on you.
Then, when you return to your own country and your position of authority, be whatever you wish.”
The next morning, the blessed man hurried to enter the king’s presence.
As he was entering, all the Magi and the nobles of the kingdom gathered and [?].
They threatened him and gnashed their teeth. But the blessed man looked at them modestly,
and softly sang this psalm: “All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I destroyed them.
They encircled me and surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I destroyed them.
They surrounded me like bees and were extinguished like a fire among dry grass, and in the name of the Lord I destroyed them.”
When he entered the king’s presence, the king called out loudly to him, “Welcome, victorious soldier, glory of our kingdom!
We have heard of your victories and have greatly praised your skill, and we are ready to reward you with honor.
But we have heard something very troubling, and if—heaven forbid!—it is true, you deserve a bitter death.”
For they say, “You have abandoned the great religion of the Magi, insulted the gods, joined the Nazarenes, and become a Nazarene.”
While the king was saying these things to him, he was signaling to him with his eyes to deny it, saying, “These things are not true, and I am not a Nazarene.”
But the blessed Qardagh secretly called upon God to be his helper. He pondered in his heart that saying
of the blessed David: “I will speak righteously before kings and will not be ashamed.”
He boldly opened his mouth and said to the king, “Truly, my lord the king, I am a true Christian.
I have confessed and continue to confess, in secret and openly, that I am a Christian.
Through the power of Christ my Lord, I defeated the enemies and destroyed the camps of the raiders
who dared to attack the territories of your dominion, those which you entrusted to me.” When the king heard these things, he was deeply distressed.
But because of the nobles of the kingdom, he made his face show anger and fury.
He said to the holy man, “Because you have denied before us the gods who govern heaven and earth
and confessed Jesus, whom the Jews crucified, we too will renounce our love for you
and erase affection for you from our minds. We will hand you over to death, to bitter deaths.”
The nobles and all the Magi raised their voices and shouted, “This man deserves ten thousand deaths!”
The king immediately ordered that he be bound hand and foot and sent to his own region to be tried there.
He did this because he thought that, while he was held in chains for a long time, he might perhaps change his mind, renounce Christianity, and live.
The chief Magus pleaded that he be handed over to him, so that he himself could judge him according to the enormity of his offense. But the king did not
answer him, because he wanted to keep the holy man alive.
The king gave orders, and they handed him over to a hundred cavalrymen, fifty foot soldiers, and twenty nobles,
to take him to the territories over which he had exercised authority, so that he could be tried there.
He wrote an edict to Gushnazdad and Dingushnasp, the chief Magian priests of those territories, as follows:
“Qardagh, who hates his own life, was honored by us with high offices, as you know.
We made him viceroy and appointed him governor of the frontier in those territories. But he denied the gods,
despised our kingship, insulted our religion, confessed Jesus who was crucified, and became a Nazarene.
We have now sent him to you in strong chains and under reliable guards,
ordering that he be given seven months to reflect and repent.
And if, within the appointed time, he does not turn away from the evil religion of the Nazarenes,
and uproot, with his own hands and the hands of his household members, the churches and monasteries he built, and rebuild the fire temples,
and purify himself through the Magi, hold the sacred twigs, make offerings to the gods, and worship the sun
and the moon and fire, we have commanded that he be stoned at the gate of his house. His blood shall be on his own head, and we are innocent of his blood.
When the king’s letters reached Gushnazdad and Dengushnasp, the chief Magi,
and they read the decree written concerning Saint Mar Qardagh, they arose in haste and brought him to Burzmihr,
who held authority over the territory westward from Nisibis, because he was a military commander and was stationed on the frontier.
When they reached Nisibis and this Burzmihr heard about it,
he assembled all the Magi in the city, men of prominence, and they went out to meet him and brought him in.
They all tried to persuade him to return to paganism and remain in his position of authority, according to the king’s command.
But he said to them, “From now on I am a Christian, and I do not worship the sun and the moon as you do.”
When he would not be persuaded by them, they set out to bring him to Shahrkhwast the judge,
who had been appointed by the king to oversee this matter, so that anyone who renounced the religion of the Magi would be handed over to him.
When they reached the place opposite the monastery of Saint Mar Yahb, it was already evening. Pagans,
however, were numerous along that river beside the monastery of Saint Mar Yahb
and in the villages around it. This Shahrkhwast lived there, and he was exceedingly wicked in his paganism.
He had inflicted many tortures on Christians to turn them back to paganism. This man came out to meet Saint Mar Qardagh.
When he saw him, he said to him, “I will not bow down to you, because you have abandoned the religion of the Magi and become a Christian.
But listen to me: worship the sun and the moon, and have yourself purified by the Magi,
and hold the sacred twigs as you used to do. Otherwise, you have much to suffer at my hands.”
But the blessed man said to him, “May Christ, whom I have confessed, rebuke you, you [?] dog!”
When he said this to him, the judge became very angry.
Immediately the judge gave orders, and they put the former bonds and irons on his legs.
He commanded them to bring instruments of torture and set them before him: pincers, branding irons, an iron comb, and the rest of the other instruments of torture.
They put an iron chain around his neck and inflicted many blows and lashes on him.
On that very night there appeared to him Saint
Abdisho, his teacher, Beri the ascetic, and the blessed martyr Saint Sergius. They said to him, “Be strong and do not be afraid, Mar Qardagh.”
Then he was released from those bonds, and he rose and prayed [?] with the saints.
They encouraged him, marked him with the sign of the cross, and departed.
But until morning came, he did not cease praying and pleading with God.
He was preparing to receive the glorious crown of martyrdom in that very place.
He prayed before God and said, “Lord God Almighty, King of kings and Lord of lords,
make me worthy to be counted among your worshipers and to join the assemblies of those who praise you.
And everyone who comes and seeks refuge in this place, asks for prayer, and remembers my name here—
may every request he makes be answered from the treasury of your mercy. Whether it concerns sickness in people or in livestock,
may he find health and healing from the abundant riches of your grace.”
When morning came, all the pagans gathered and threatened him, saying,
“If he does not worship the sun, we will put him to a bitter death.”
But he said to them, “Go away from me, children of hell! I worship Christ the King,
for he is God of gods and Lord of lords.” When the judge heard this, he wanted them to kill him there.
But because of the king’s command, which stipulated, “If within seven months he does not repent and return to the religion of the Magi,
have himself purified by the Magi, rebuild the fire temple he demolished, hold the sacred barsom branches, and perform the Magian rites,
he is to be stoned before the gate of his house,” they could not violate the king’s command and kill him there.
The chief Magian priests, too, would not agree to this.
Instead, they immediately brought him to his house, so that he would die there according to the king’s command.
When the blessed man reached the meeting place of his fortress beside the village of Melqi, he raised his eyes and saw his fortress and his house.
He lifted his gaze to heaven and stretched his [?] upward toward God. He prayed and said, “Christ, my hope,
you gave your body to the cross and your hands and feet to be pierced with nails for the salvation of our race.
You freed Adam and his children from the bonds of death. Free me also from these bonds, and rescue me from the nations that have gone astray,
so that those who hate me may see and be ashamed, because you, Lord, have helped and comforted me.” At that very moment the bonds fell from his hands.
And from his feet [?]. He turned and bowed toward the east. He stretched out his hands to heaven and gave thanks to God.
When the nobles, the pagans, and the foot soldiers saw what had happened, some of them fled in haste and scattered in various directions.
Others ran and hid among the reeds and rushes of the lake beside the blessed man’s fortress.
But he went up to his fortress and entered his house, rejoicing and praising God.
He encouraged his wife, his sister, and everyone in his household. He gave orders to the guards and stationed lookouts on the wall of his fortress.
When the king learned of this, he was greatly disturbed. He gnashed his teeth in anger and roared like a ravening lion.
Immediately he wrote a royal decree to Burzmihr-Shapur, the commander of the army of the west,
ordering him to send companies of cavalry to capture the blessed man’s fortress, seize him, and stone him on the ground in front of his fortress.
If the cavalry he sent could not seize the blessed man and capture his fortress, the commander himself was to come with his entire army
and attack the fortress and capture it. The commander immediately sent twenty companies of soldiers.
They besieged the blessed man’s fortress for a month but accomplished nothing. Many of them died
in the fighting, for he flashed against them like powerful lightning from the wall of his fortress,
and with his sharp arrows he brought many of them down. Then the commander himself came with his entire army, but they accomplished nothing.
Then they wrote to inform the king: “Unless he is seized through stratagems, cunning, and persuasion,
he cannot be captured by force and fighting.” The king gave orders, and the armies withdrew.
Ten companies remained, encamped two or three miles away from the blessed man’s fortress.
Then, at the king’s command, the nobles of his own people gathered
to persuade him to surrender, so that his fathers and brothers would not perish because of him.
When they had gathered and arrived, the blessed man went up onto the wall of his fortress and said to them:
“Why are you troubling yourselves, men? Why have you gathered?” They bowed to him from a distance and wept.
They all said to him with one voice, “Have pity, my lord, on yourself and on us as well.
Do not oppose the king, and do not leave our renowned family with a bad name.
Instead, order the gate of the fortress to be opened and come out to us.
Obey the king’s command and bow down just once to the fire
and the sun [?]. Save your life and deliver us too. Afterward, live as you wish.”
But the blessed man opened his mouth and said to them, “If only you too would have pity on yourselves,
just as I have pity on you. Because I truly had pity on myself,
I have rescued my soul from the jaws of the error in which you are trapped, and brought it to Christ, the light of the world.
And I am ready to endure ten thousand deaths for his holy name.
If you listen to me, you too will be found worthy along with me.
We will present a single company of martyrs to Christ God, ascend to heaven, and delight with him in that life which never ends.
As for your saying, ‘Do not stand up against the king,’ you have truly spoken like old women.
For which is harder: to stand against a wretched human being who flourishes and is puffed up today, but tomorrow is gone,
or to stand against the heavenly King of kings, whose kingdom does not pass away
and whose divinity does not change? For as long as I was held in error like you,
and did not know Christ my Lord, the sure hope of my life,
I served the pagan and wicked king and fought bravely in his battles. But now,
since I have come to know Christ as the heavenly King and the sure hope,
I will not serve mortal kings who are led astray, nor am I afraid of their threats.”
When they heard him insult the king and call him wicked and misguided, they all shouted, stopped their ears, and said to one another:
“Let us get away! Let us get away, and not hear blasphemy against the revered King of kings!” But the blessed man laughed and said to them:
“You truly are wretched! You blaspheme God, the creator and sustainer of the worlds,
and offer the worship owed to him to his mute images [?],
and flatter a mortal man who is far (and far) from God.”
While he was speaking with them, Gushnazdad and Dingushnasp, the chief priests, arrived with other Magi.
They approached the blessed man’s fortress and said to him, “We do not bow down to you,
because you have insulted the gods, stood up against the King of kings, and become a Nazarene.
But listen to what the King of kings has commanded us in letters concerning you.
The merciful King of kings has commanded: ‘Worship fire, the sun, and the moon.
Rebuild the fire temple you tore down, demolish the churches and monasteries you built, and purify yourself in the assembly of the Magi.
Take up the barsom twigs, live and do not die, and retain your authority.
But the blessed Qardagh became indignant and said to them, “Shut your mouths, you unclean and loathsome servants of Satan!
Far be it from me to abandon the true God, who made heaven and earth, and worship mute created things.
I regard the unclean commands of your pagan king as blasphemies that demons brazenly utter against God.”
When the Magi heard these things, they retreated, wailing and crying out,
“Who can bear to hear blasphemy against the King of Kings?” But one of them, named Sibarzad, bent down and picked up dust from the ground,
threw it toward the blessed man, and said, “This is for that mouth that blasphemed against the gods and against the King of Kings!”
But the blessed man signaled to one of his servants to give him a bow and a single arrow.
He secretly took hold of his bow in the shadow of one of the wall’s battlements and fitted an arrow to it.
He drew the bow and struck that Magus in the mouth. The arrow came out behind him, and he fell and died on the spot.
The blessed man laughed and said to him, “Receive your reward for your love for your gods and your king!” Then all the Magi fled
in haste, wailing, and the nobles of his own family departed in sorrow.
Then the blessed Qardagh called [?] one of them, named Anosh, a man praised for his knowledge and uprightness,
and said to him, “Do you suppose, Anosh,
that I am afraid of death for Christ’s sake and that this is why I remain in the fortress? No, far be it from me! That is not so.
For death for Christ’s sake is sweeter to me than this present life.
But until Christ himself commands me, either in a dream or in a vision of the night,
that it is time for me to die for his name, I will not surrender myself to men afflicted by error.
I trust in the power of Christ my Lord that no one can harm me.
But when it pleases Christ that I should die for his sake, I will go out joyfully and surrender myself to be killed.”
When the king learned of these things, he sent written orders to Nekorgan, who was the blessed man’s father-in-law,
that he should go and persuade him to open the gate of his fortress and surrender.
If he did not accomplish this, Nekorgan himself would suffer a sentence [?] of bitter death. So Nekorgan came and camped at a distance from
the blessed man’s fortress, about two bowshots away, for he was afraid to approach the fortress any closer.
He sent word to the blessed man to come up onto the wall and speak with him.
Then the blessed man went up, sat opposite him, and said to him, “Come here, old man, and do not be afraid.”
When he came near, he said to him, “Why are you distressed, Nekhorgan? And why have you come here?” He wept bitterly and said to him:
“I am distressed by the misfortunes that have befallen me, for I have lost a son-in-law who had no equal among men.
And now death threatens me too, unless you open the fortress gate and give me a helping hand.”
But the blessed man said to him, “Because your mind is lost in the deception of demons, you think that I am utterly lost.
But if your mind were not lost, you would understand that I have not perished [?],
but have indeed been found by Christ, who finds the lost [?].
You are the one who is truly lost, for you have abandoned God the Creator, and it is mute created things—
things created for your honor and enjoyment—that you worship.”
Nekhorgan said to him, “Think of me however you wish, and insult me as much as you like.
Only save me from death, for the king of kings is angrily threatening me because of you.
Do one of two things: either obey the king, abandon Christianity, and return
to the religion of the Magi; worship fire, the sun, and the moon; rebuild the fire temple you destroyed, and live.
Or go out and die, as foolish Christians die, so that we do not die because of you.”
The blessed Qardagh answered him, “I will not obey the pagan and wicked king.
I will not abandon God, who created me, saved me, provides for me, and will give me joy in his kingdom.
I will not worship created things as you do. Nor will I shrink from dying for Christ.
Instead, I will die gladly, and you will not die in my place.
If only you had understanding and would die for the sake of your own lives!
As for your calling the Christians who die for the name of their Lord [?] fools, you spoke from the depths of your madness.
But sit down, and do not be anxious or sad. I am now pleading with Christ my Lord
to show me whether it is time for me to die for his name. And if it accords with the will of his divinity,
and it is time to receive the crown of martyrdom at the end of this struggle for his sake,
I will gladly go out and surrender myself to the executioners.”
Then the news spread throughout all the territories under the blessed man’s authority: “Qardagh is ready to die for the name of Christ.”
And great crowds gathered and came from every region,
Christians, Jews, and pagans, and they set up large camps beside the blessed man's fortress,
waiting to see the day when the champion of righteousness would receive his crown.
His parents and brothers also came, and there were great camps of thousands and tens of thousands.
They remained encamped for twenty-one days. Meanwhile, the blessed man persisted in prayer and supplication,
begging the one who appointed the contest to strengthen and encourage him to attain perfection through the crown of martyrdom.
His father pleaded with him at length, weeping,
asking him to come up onto the wall, see him, speak with him, and hear what he wanted to tell him.
But he refused. Instead, he sent him a message through one of his servants, saying, “Christ our Lord calls out to us in his Gospel:
‘Anyone who does not leave father and mother, brothers and sisters, wife and children, and come after me is not worthy of me.’
For this reason I do not wish to see your face,
because your thoughts and words oppose this path that I am preparing to travel.”
After this, Nekorgan sent him a message: “Send me my daughter Shushan, for I long to see her.”
The blessed man said to his wife, “Go out to your father and see what he wants of you.
Yet I know that the destruction of your life
is what you will gain from his words.” When she went out to her father, he said to her, “My daughter, my beloved,
have pity on me in my old age. Do not exchange your father's love for love of your husband.
Do not trade away my life in my old age for a man who has rebelled against the gods and the King of Kings.
For there is no possibility of your obtaining another father. But if your husband dies today, tomorrow you can find someone better than he is.
Instead, persuade him to open the gate and come out, so that we may escape danger.”
She immediately returned to the blessed man and said to him, “If you are a Christian,
go out courageously and die bravely, as Christians die.
Why are you shut up here in the fortress like cowards who fear death,
while many are dying because of you?” The blessed man answered her,
“Truly, the lips speak from the abundance of the heart, according to the life-giving word of our Savior.”
And these things you are saying are the evil devices of paganism, the fruits of wickedness, and the words of the deceitful one.
But do not trouble yourself, daughter of destruction, for I am ready to die, even before your deceitful enticements.
After all these things, a terrifying vision appeared to the blessed man.
On the night before Friday dawned, the blessed man rose and performed his customary service of prayer.
When he finished his service as morning was growing light, he turned and saw himself standing on a small hill before the gate of his fortress,
with great crowds of people surrounding him and showering him with pearls.
As the pearls fell on his body, drops of blood splashed out from the places where they struck,
and they were transformed into torches of fire and went up to heaven. And a man dressed in radiant clothes,
and crowned with a crown of light, stood above him in the air and said to him, “My brother Qardagh!” He answered, “Here I am.”
He said to him, “These pearls were showered upon me too in Jerusalem, by members of my own people and my own family.
Now let your father come and throw a single pearl at you himself, and immediately you will ascend to me in joy.”
Then the blessed Qardagh asked him, “Who are you, my lord?” He said to him:
“I am Stephen the deacon, who was stoned in Jerusalem for proclaiming life.”
Immediately the blessed man awoke with a start and was greatly afraid.
He called Isaac his teacher, who used to teach him the Psalms and read the holy Scriptures to him, and recounted
to him the vision he had seen. In amazement they considered the vision,
and understood that the time had now come for the blessed man to die by stoning for the name of Christ.
The blessed Qardagh said to Isaac, “Where is the account of Stephen [?] written?” Isaac said to him:
“It is written in the Acts of the Holy Apostles.” The blessed man said to him, “Bring it and read it to me.”
When he heard the account of Saint Stephen’s martyrdom, he rejoiced greatly, and his soul was glad.
He took courage and became very strong. He longed to die for Christ,
like a thirsty man who comes in from a journey in the heat of summer and longs for cold water.
Immediately the blessed man rose, knelt down, and prayed.
He kissed the book of the holy Gospel and marked himself with the sign of the cross.
He opened the gate of his fortress and went out like a bridegroom coming out of his bridal chamber.
When this became known to the crowds, a commotion broke out in the camps, and everyone hurried there:
Christians, Jews, and pagans, great and small, men and women.
They were running to see the blessed man receive the crown of martyrdom.
The horsemen, mounted and armed, rushed about, pressuring the crowds
and saying, “Everyone must take a stone and stone the blessed man.”
The Magi gathered with all the nobles. They sat down and read the document containing the blessed man’s sentence,
which had been sent by the king—the document that the church customarily calls a “katarasis,” while the Persians call it a “nebeshtag.”
When the blessed man himself saw the crowds of pagans and Jews carrying stones
and running to stone him, he looked up to heaven and made the sign of the cross over himself.
He prayed aloud and said, “Our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, help me at this hour,
and make me worthy to join the assemblies of your saints with confidence.” Immediately he knelt down.
When a heap of stones had risen over him, he shook them off and stood up valiantly. He did the same a second time.
While the horsemen and the Magi were pressuring the crowds to throw stones forcefully,
the blessed man spoke up and said to them, “I will not die unless my father throws a stone at me.”
His father, intoxicated by the errors of the Magian religion, afraid of death, and seeking to please the king and the nobles, took
his headcloth, wrapped it around his face, and threw a stone in the stoning of his son.
Immediately the soul of this champion of righteousness departed to eternal life.
At that very hour, the fragrance of spices spread throughout the place where the blessed man had been stoned.
And a voice was heard saying, “You have fought well and conquered valiantly, victorious Qardagh! Come with joy and receive the crown of your victory.”
Saint Mar Qardagh was crowned in the forty-ninth year of King Shapur, on a Friday.
That same night, before Saturday dawned, compassionate men gathered
and snatched the saint’s body away from his guards and buried him with great honor.
Every year, on the day when the blessed man had been crowned, people would gather at the place where he had been crowned,
and celebrate a festival and commemoration for him for three days.
Because the crowds were so large, they even began to buy and sell during the days
Of the commemoration of the saint. And as time went on:
A great festival was held at the place where the blessed man was stoned, and continues to this day.
The saint’s commemoration lasts three days, and the festival six days.
It is called the Market of Malqi, after the name of the village of the blessed man’s fortress.
Afterward, a great and beautiful church was also built at great expense in the blessed man’s name,
by believers who wished to be remembered favorably, beside that hill on which the holy Mar Qardagh was stoned.
May we be worthy to receive help through his prayers in this world full of sorrows,
and in that new world which does not pass away, may we receive mercy through his prayers and enjoy delight with him,
through the grace and compassion of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, and to his Father and the Holy Spirit,
be praise, honor, and exaltation forever and ever. Amen.
The martyrdom of Mar Qardagh, the holy and victorious martyr, is ended. (4) Afterward, the believers brought gold and silver,
and built four churches for him, and another church for the martyrs’ shrine,
and an altar, sanctuaries, and a baptistery. And it was consecrated on the eastern side.
Great sums were spent on it in the blessed man’s name by believers who wished to be remembered favorably.
And whoever [?] a commemoration for him on the day on which he was stoned, may he be worthy to have a share with that blessed man and a good end.
